$$ \text{Pr}(|\bra{0}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}\tilde{P}_{\alpha}C_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}|=1)=\frac{1}{2^{2N}}+(1-\frac{1}{2^{2N}})\frac{1}{2^{N}}=\frac{1+\frac{1}{2^{N}}-\frac{1}{2^{2N}}}{2^{N}}, $$

and $\text{Pr}(\bra{0}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}C_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C_{t+1}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}=0)\geq 1-\frac{1}{2^{N}}-\frac{1}{2^{2N}}.$ ∎

#### Lemma II.3.

For randomly selected Clifford circuits $\{C_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ and Pauli operators $P_{\alpha}$ , $P_{\beta}$ , assuming that $P_{\alpha}=P_{\beta}$ and $t=t^{\prime}$ are not simultaneously true,

$$ \displaystyle\Pr(\bra{z}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|C_{1}\cdots C_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{1}|z}=0)\geq 1-\frac{1}{2^{N}}. $$

Proof. By the same logic as in Lemma II.1, we can write $\braket{0|C_{1}\cdots C_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{1}|z}=\delta_{z,z^{\prime}}$ , where $z^{\prime}$ satisfies $C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}C_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\propto\ket{z^{\prime}}$ . As before, we first compute $\text{Pr}(|\bra{z}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|C_{1}\cdots C_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{1}|z}|=1)$ . This only occurs if $C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\propto\ket{z^{\prime}}$ . Now, there are $2\times 2^{N}$ elements $\tilde{P}$ of the Pauli group for which $\tilde{P}\ket{0}=\ket{z^{\prime}}$ (omitting those with imaginary phase, as they cannot be reached by Clifford conjugation from Pauli strings). Specifically, to construct $\tilde{P}$ , we choose $\mathds{1}$ or $Z$ for the qubits $j$ where $z^{\prime}_{j}=0$ , either $X$ or $Y$ for the qubits $j$ where $z^{\prime}_{j}=1$ , and one of two phases $\pm 1$ . Thus, $\text{Pr}(|\bra{z}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|C_{1}\cdots C_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{1}|z}|=1)=\frac{2\times 2^{N}}{2\times 2^{2N}}=\frac{1}{2^{N}}$ . So, $\text{Pr}(\bra{z}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|C_{1}\cdots C_{t^{\prime}}P_{\beta}C^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{1}|z}=0)=1-\frac{1}{2^{N}}$ . ∎

Based on these results, we can now establish the derivatives

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\theta_{\alpha}(t)}p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})|_{\vec{\theta}=0,\vec{\gamma}=0}=0, \displaystyle\partial_{\theta_{\alpha}(t),\theta(t^{\prime})_{\beta}}p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})|_{\vec{\theta}=0,\vec{\gamma}=0} \displaystyle=\big(-2|\braket{0|z}|^{2}+2|\braket{0|C_{1}\cdots C_{t}P_{\alpha}C^{\dagger}_{t}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{1}|z}|^{2}\big)\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\delta_{t,t^{\prime}} $$

with exponentially high probability. Specifically, the first equation comes using Lemma II.1 with Eq. (II.4), while the second comes from applying Lemmas II.2 and II.3 to Eq. (II.6).

Defining

$$ \displaystyle k_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle\equiv\lvert\bra{z}C_{1}^{\dagger}...C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}...C_{1}\ket{0}\rvert^{2}, \displaystyle p_{0}(z) \displaystyle\equiv|\braket{0|z}|^{2}, $$

we see that we can approximate $p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})$ perturbatively as

$$ \displaystyle p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma}) \displaystyle\approx A\big(p_{0}(z)+\sum_{\beta,t}\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}k_{\beta,t}(z)+\sum_{\alpha,t}\theta_{\alpha}(t)^{2}k_{\alpha,t}(z)\big) \displaystyle\approx A\big(p_{0}(z)+\sum_{\beta,t}\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}k_{\beta,t}(z)\big), $$

where we drop higher-order terms in $\theta^{2}_{\alpha}$ and

$$ \displaystyle A=\prod_{\alpha,t}\cos^{2}(\theta_{\alpha}(t))\prod_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(1-\gamma_{\beta}(t^{\prime})) $$

is the probability that no signal occurs. Note that in our expansion above, $A\approx 1-\sum_{\alpha,t}\theta_{\alpha}(t)^{2}-\sum_{\beta,t}\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ . The first term in Eq. (II.11), for example, contributes to $Ap_{0}(z)$ . For a more extensive discussion of the renormalization $A$ , see Section I.1. Here, we have assumed coherent signals couple to the system via operators $\{P_{\alpha}\}$ , while incoherent signals couple to the system via different operators $\{P_{\beta}\}$ for simplicity. However, our analysis can be easily extended to when they are present with the same Pauli generators (see Sec. II.1.7).

We also establish that $k_{\beta,t}(z)$ is supported on a single bitstring, as stated in the main text. This property will play an important role in demonstrating the robustness of our approach.

#### Theorem II.1.

For any set Clifford circuits $\{C_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ drawn uniformly at random and a Pauli operator $P_{\alpha}$ ,

$$ k_{\alpha,t}(z)=\lvert\bra{z}C_{1}^{\dagger}...C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}...C_{1}\ket{0}\rvert^{2} $$

is supported on a single bitstring.

Proof— $C_{1}^{\dagger}...C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}...C_{1}\ket{0}\propto\ket{z^{\prime}}$ for some bitstring $z^{\prime}$ . Thus, $\lvert\bra{z}C_{1}^{\dagger}...C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}...C_{1}\ket{0}\rvert^{2}=\delta_{z,z^{\prime}}$ . This is a distribution which is supported only on $z^{\prime}$ , $k_{\alpha,t}(z^{\prime})=1$ . ∎

Now, if each $k_{\beta,t}(z)$ are supported on different bitstrings, then it is easy to see from Eq. (II.15) that all signals $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ will be distinguishable from the measured distribution. Indeed, this is the same principle we used in quadratic sensing (Section I.1). For a single set of Clifford operators $\{C_{t}\}^{T}_{t=1}$ on an $N$ -qubit system, we can constrain the probability of failure of our protocol—when two or more signals map to the same bitstring. The following theorem shows that a successful protocol requires $N=O(\log K_{ic}^{2})$ .

#### Theorem II.2.

For a single set of Clifford operators $\{C_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ drawn uniformly at random and $K_{ic}>1$ incoherent Pauli signals on an $N-$ qubit system, the probability of a collision (when two or more signals are indistinguishable), defined as

$$ \mathsf{Coll}:=\Big\{\exists\,(\alpha,t)\neq(\beta,t^{\prime})\ \text{such that}\ k_{\alpha,t}(z)=k_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)\,\forall z\Big\}, $$

satisfies

$$ \Pr(\mathsf{Coll})\;\leq\;\binom{K_{ic}}{2}\,2^{-N}\;\leq\;\frac{(K_{ic})^{2}}{2^{N+1}}. $$

Proof— For any fixed pair $(\alpha,t)\neq(\beta,t^{\prime})$ , uniform randomness of the support of $k_{\alpha,t}(z)$ and $k_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)$ implies

$$ \Pr\!\left[k_{\alpha,t}(z)=k_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)\right]=2^{-N}. $$

Applying a union bound over all $\binom{K_{ic}}{2}$ distinct pairs yields

$$ \Pr(\mathsf{Coll})\leq\sum_{(\alpha,t)\neq(\beta,t^{\prime})}\Pr\!\left[k_{\alpha,t}(z)=k_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)\right]=\binom{K_{ic}}{2}\,2^{-N}, $$

which implies the stated bound. ∎

This means that to guarantee success probability at least $1-\delta$ (i.e., $\Pr(\mathsf{Coll})\leq\delta$ ), it suffices to choose $N$ such that

$$ \binom{K_{ic}}{2}\,2^{-N}\leq\delta,\qquad\text{e.g.,}\qquad N\geq\log\bigg(\frac{K_{ic}(K_{ic}-1)}{2\delta}\bigg). $$

In particular, achieving success probability $1-\delta$ requires $N$ to grow logarithmically with $K_{ic}^{2}$ .

Although we can suppress the probability of error by increasing the system size $N$ , it is also useful to be able to ensure accuracy at a fixed system size. We therefore allow selecting multiple sets of Clifford circuits to run in our protocol. Theorem II.3 shows that, in this case, a sucessful protocol requires $n_{c}=O(\log(K_{ic}^{2})/N)$ sets of Clifford circuits.

#### Theorem II.3.

Fix $n_{c}$ sets of Clifford circuits drawn uniformly randomly, denoted $\mathrm{C}_{n}\equiv\{C^{(n)}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ for $n=1,\dots,n_{c}$ . Let $k^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ be defined as in Eq. (II.12) calculated for the circuit $\mathrm{C}_{n}$ . Then, the probability of a collision over all $n_{c}$ circuits, such that there exists $(\alpha,t)\neq(\beta,t^{\prime})$ such that

$$ k^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=k^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)\quad\text{for all }n\in\{1,\dots,n_{c}\}, $$

is bounded as

$$ \Pr\!\left[\exists\;(\alpha,t)\neq(\beta,t^{\prime})\text{ s.t. }k^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=k^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)\ \forall n\right]\;\leq\;\binom{K_{ic}}{2}\,2^{-Nn_{c}}\;=\;\frac{K_{ic}(K_{ic}-1)}{2}\,2^{-Nn_{c}}. $$

Proof— For $n_{c}$ circuits, failure occurs when two or more signals are indistinguishable in every circuit. For any given two signals $\gamma_{\alpha}(t)$ , $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ , the probability that they are indistinguishable in a single circuit is $\frac{1}{2^{N}}$ . Thus, the probability $\Pr(\text{failure})$ that there is indistinguishability across any two signals for all $n_{c}$ circuits is $\Pr(\text{failure})\leq\begin{pmatrix}K_{ic}\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2^{Nn_{c}}}$ = $\frac{K_{ic}(K_{ic}-1)}{2}\frac{1}{2^{Nn_{c}}}$ , where we have used a union bound over all pairs of signals. ∎

This implies that to guarantee success probability at least $1-\delta$ , it suffices to choose $n_{c}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{K_{ic}(K_{ic}-1)}{2}\,2^{-Nn_{c}}\leq\delta,\qquad\text{e.g.,}\qquad n_{c}\geq\log\left(\frac{K_{ic}(K_{ic}-1)}{2\delta}\right)/N. $$

To control the failure probability $\delta$ of incoherent multiparameter estimation for a given $N$ , we thus choose the number of circuits $n_{c}$ based on Theorem II.3. Now, when we run $n_{c}$ circuits, we will have $n_{c}$ different relations of the form Eq. (II.15). To construct our estimator for $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ , we simply invert all of these equations simultaneously using linear regression [5].

Specifically, we think of $p^{(n)}_{0}(z)$ and $k^{(n)}_{\beta,t}(z)$ each as $2^{N}$ dimensional vectors over bitstrings $z$ , where the superscript indicates the circuit iteration considered. Note that for every circuit $\mathrm{C}_{n}$ , $p^{(n)}_{0}(0)=1$ . We then concatenate of these vectors vertically across circuits to form $n_{c}\times 2^{N}$ dimensional vectors:

$$ \displaystyle k^{all}_{\beta,t}(\tilde{z})\equiv\begin{bmatrix}k^{(1)}_{\beta,t}(z^{(1)})\\
\vdots\\
k^{(n_{c})}_{\beta,t}(z^{(n_{c})})\end{bmatrix},\,\,p^{all}_{0}(\tilde{z})\equiv\begin{bmatrix}p^{(1)}_{0}(z^{(1)})\\
\vdots\\
p^{(n_{c})}_{0}(z^{(n_{c})})\end{bmatrix}. $$

Here, $z^{(n)}$ indicates the bitstring $z$ drawn from the circuit $\mathrm{C}_{n}$ , while $\tilde{z}$ represents bitstrings from any circuit. After forming these super vectors, we can concatenate them horizontally to form a $n_{c}2^{N}\times(K_{ic}+1)$ dimensional matrix $V$ . Here, $K_{ic}$ is the number of incoherent signals $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ . The columns of $V$ are given by $V_{\tilde{z},0}=p^{all}_{0}(\tilde{z})$ , and $V_{z,\beta t}=k^{all}_{\beta,t}(\tilde{z})$ , where we combine $\beta$ and $t$ into a single index. Then, we see that $p(\tilde{z}|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})=AV_{\tilde{z},0}+A\sum_{\beta t}V_{\tilde{z},\beta t}\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}$ , where we implicitly assume $\beta t$ runs from $1$ to $K_{ic}$ . An estimator for $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ can then be obtained by inverting this equation using least-squares regression, replacing $p(\tilde{z}|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})$ with the empirical distribution:

$$ \displaystyle v_{{ic},{\beta t}}=\sum_{i,\tilde{z}}(V^{T}V)^{-1}_{\beta t,i}V^{T}_{i,\tilde{z}}\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M/n_{c}},\;\;\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)=\frac{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}+v_{{ic},{0}}},\;\;\hat{A}=v_{ic,0} $$

$\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}$ is again formed by concatenating across circuits,

$$ \displaystyle\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}=\begin{bmatrix}\hat{N}_{z^{(1)}}\\
\vdots\\
\hat{N}_{z^{(n_{c})}}\end{bmatrix}, $$

where $\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}$ indicates the number of times bitstring $z$ is measured for circuit $n$ . So, for instance, $\sum_{\tilde{z}}k^{all}_{\beta,t}(\tilde{z})\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M/n_{c}}=\sum_{z,n}k^{(n)}_{\beta,t}(z)\frac{\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}}{M/n_{c}}$ . Note that we sample $\frac{M}{n_{c}}$ times for each circuit, for a total of $M$ samples. This estimator is unbiased up to higher-order corrections in the signals, and for the rest of our analysis, we assume $\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)$ is indeed unbiased, instead operating in the regime where statistical error dominates over bias—relevant for small $M$ . Corrections to this assumption can be obtained by including contributions from both bias and variance in the error of the estimator, and further discussion of the behavior of the bias is given in Sec. II.1.8.

Now, although our estimator is defined in terms of a $n_{c}2^{N}\times(K_{ic}+1)$ dimensional matrix $V$ , we do not ever need to construct this matrix in practice. Instead, we can directly compute the elements of the $(K_{ic}+1)\times(K_{ic}+1)$ matrix $V^{T}V$ , which can be done efficiently. Consequently, the overall data-analysis procedure is polynomial in all relevant parameters, as shown in Theorem II.4.

#### Theorem II.4.

The classical complexity of computing $\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)$ (Eq. (II.20)) is $O(K_{ic}n_{c}N^{2}+K_{ic}^{2}n_{c}+K_{ic}^{3}+K_{ic}M)$ .

Proof. We first compute each of the $n_{c}\times K_{ic}$ perturbations $k^{(n)}_{\beta,t}(z)$ . By Theorem II.1, each is supported on a single bitstring, so we just need to compute $C_{1}^{\dagger}...C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\beta}C_{t}...C_{1}$ in the stabilizer formalism and find the non- $Z,I$ term. This costs $n_{c}\times K_{ic}\times N^{2}$ , ignoring $\log N$ factors for search.

We then construct $V^{T}V$ . Each entry of $V^{T}V$ is given by the inner product of two sparse vectors with $n_{c}$ nonzero entries. Thus, this costs $n_{c}(K_{ic}+1)^{2}$ . Inverting the $(K_{ic}+1)\times(K_{ic}+1)$ dimensional matrix $V^{T}V$ costs $(K_{ic}+1)^{3}$ .

Finally, we only compute $V^{T}_{i,\tilde{z}}\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M/n_{c}}$ for each $\tilde{z}$ that we have sampled. As we have $M$ total samples and $K_{ic}+1$ total rows $i$ of $V^{T}$ , this costs time $K_{ic}M$ . ∎

Coherent signals— Recall that to determine coherent signals using the Clifford procedure, we must measure in the $x-$ basis at the end. This ensures that the first-order perturbation in $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ is not zero, as is the case in the incoherent protocol (c.f. Eq. (II.10)). This results in first-order terms

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\theta_{\alpha}(t)}p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})|_{\vec{\theta}=0,\vec{\gamma}=0} \displaystyle=2\im\big[\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}\big]\equiv\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle\partial_{\gamma_{\alpha}(t)}p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})|_{\vec{\theta}=0,\vec{\gamma}=0} \displaystyle=\lvert\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}C_{1}^{\dagger}...C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}...C_{1}\ket{0}\rvert^{2}-\lvert\braket{z|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|0}\rvert^{2}=0. $$

As before, we can examine the structure of these terms. We can rewrite Eq. (II.23) as $\lvert\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}\ket{z^{\prime}}\rvert^{2}-\lvert\braket{z|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|0}\rvert^{2}$ , where $C_{1}^{\dagger}...C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}...C_{1}\ket{0}\propto\ket{z^{\prime}}$ . In this form, we see that both terms will lead to a uniform distribution over all bitstrings $z$ , so they cancel to zero: the coherent protocol is insensitive to incoherent signals to first order. Meanwhile, Eq. (II.22) may sometimes evaluate to zero, as we show below.

#### Theorem II.5.

For a set of Clifford circuits $\{C_{t}\}^{T}_{t=1}$ selected uniformly randomly and a fixed signal indicated by $(\alpha,t)$ , $\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z)=0$ for all bitstrings $z$ with probability $p=\frac{1}{2}$ .

Proof— We want to analyze when $\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}$ is completely real. Now, we denote $\tilde{P}_{\alpha}\equiv C^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots C^{\dagger}_{t}P_{\alpha}C_{t}\cdots C_{1}$ . We thus want to know when $\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}\tilde{P}_{\alpha}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}$ is real. $\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}$ is always real, so it depends on $\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}\tilde{P}_{\alpha}\ket{0}$ . Now, $\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}\tilde{P}_{\alpha}|z}$ is real when $\tilde{P}_{\alpha}$ contains an odd number of Pauli $Y$ . This happens with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ in the limit of large $N$ . ∎

Thus, we can approximate the output of the coherent estimation protocol for a single circuit as

$$ \displaystyle p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})\approx p_{0}(z)+A\sum_{\alpha,t}\theta_{\alpha}(t)\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z), $$

where $A=\prod_{\alpha,t}\cos^{2}(\theta_{\alpha}(t))\prod_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(1-\gamma_{\beta}(t^{\prime}))$ and $p_{0}(z)$ is the uniform distribution over all bitstrings $z$ . We note that $A$ does not renormalize the coefficient of $p_{0}(z)$ here as the terms which contribute to this renormalization cancel (see Eq. (II.23), which is equal to the term $\propto\theta^{2}_{\alpha}$ and vanishes).

Now, due to Theorem II.5, we cannot just take one set of Clifford operators $\{C_{t}\}^{T}_{t=1}$ , as there is a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$ for each signal that they have $\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z)=0$ —the circuit is not sensitive to the signal. To rectify this issue, we again consider multiple sets of Clifford circuits. Theorem II.6 shows that a successful protocol requires $n_{c}=O(\log K_{c})$ sets of Clifford circuits.

#### Theorem II.6.

Fix $n_{c}$ sets of Clifford circuits drawn uniformly randomly, denoted $\mathrm{C}_{n}\equiv\{C^{(n)}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ for $n=1,\dots,n_{c}$ . Let $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ be defined as in Eq. (II.22), calculated for the circuit $\mathrm{C}_{n}$ . Then the probability that there exists ( $\alpha$ , $t$ ) such that

$$ \delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=0\quad\text{for all }n\in\{1,\dots,n_{c}\}, $$

is given by

$$ \Pr\!\left[\exists\;\alpha,t\ \text{s.t.}\ \delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=0\ \forall n\right]=1-\big(1-2^{-n_{c}}\big)^{K_{c}}, $$

where $K_{c}$ is the total number of coherent signals $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ .

Proof. Failure occurs if there exists a coherent signal $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ whose first-order contribution $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ vanishes for every one of the $n_{c}$ circuits. For a fixed signal $\alpha$ and time $t$ , the probability that $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=0$ for a single circuit is $1/2$ . Independence of the circuits implies that the probability this occurs for all $n_{c}$ circuits is $2^{-n_{c}}$ .

Therefore, the probability that a given signal is detected (i.e., is nonzero for at least one circuit) is $1-2^{-n_{c}}$ . Requiring this to hold for all $K_{c}$ coherent signals yields

$$ \Pr(\text{success})=\big(1-2^{-n_{c}}\big)^{K_{c}}, $$

and hence the failure probability is

$$ \Pr(\text{failure})=1-\big(1-2^{-n_{c}}\big)^{K_{c}}. $$

$\square$

This implies that to guarantee a success probability of at least $1-\delta$ , it suffices to choose $n_{c}$ such that

$$ 1-\big(1-2^{-n_{c}}\big)^{K_{c}}\leq\delta. $$

For small $\delta$ , this condition implies that we need to take

$$ n_{c}\gtrsim\log_{2}\!\left(\frac{K_{c}}{\delta}\right), $$

so that the number of circuit sets required grows logarithmically with the number of coherent signals.

As before, we can control the failure probability by choosing $n_{c}$ according to Theorem II.6. When we run $n_{c}$ circuits, we will again have $n_{c}$ relations like Eq. (II.24). We can similarly invert them to obtain our estimator for $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ . This procedure is almost identical to the discussion surrounding Eq. (II.19), so we shorten the explanation here for brevity. As in Eq. (II.19), we can concatenate our $\delta p^{n}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ and $p_{0}^{(n)}(z)$ for each circuit $n$ vertically, to make $n_{c}\times 2^{N}$ dimensional vectors $p_{0}^{all}(\tilde{z})$ , $\delta p^{all}_{\alpha,t}(\tilde{z})$ . In this case, $p_{0}^{(n)}(z)$ is the uniform distribution over all bitstrings $z$ for each circuit $n$ . We then join them together horizontally to make a $n_{c}2^{N}\times(K_{c}+1)$ dimensional matrix $V$ . The columns of $V$ are $V_{\tilde{z},0}=p^{all}_{0}(\tilde{z})$ , and $V_{z,\alpha t}=\delta p^{all}_{\alpha,t}(\tilde{z})$ . Then, we see that $p(\tilde{z}|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})=V_{\tilde{z},0}+A\sum_{\alpha t}V_{\tilde{z},\alpha t}\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ , where we implicitly assume $\alpha t$ runs from $1$ to $K_{c}$ . An estimator for $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ can then be obtained by inverting this equation approximately:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)=\frac{1}{\hat{A}}\sum_{i,\tilde{z}}(V^{T}V)^{-1}_{\alpha t,i}V^{T}_{i,\tilde{z}}\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M/n_{c}} $$

where $\hat{A}$ is obtained from the incoherent estimator Eq. (II.20) and $\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}$ is defined in Eq. (II.21). This estimator is unbiased up to higher-order corrections in the signals, and for the rest of our analysis, we assume $\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)$ is indeed unbiased, instead working in the regime where statistical error dominates. Corrections to this assumption can be obtained by including contributions from both bias and variance in the error of the estimator, and further discussion of the behavior of the bias is given in Sec. II.1.8.

Now, although our estimator is defined in terms of an $n_{c}2^{N}\times(K_{c}+1)$ dimensional matrix $V$ , we do not ever need to construct this matrix in practice. Instead, we can directly compute the entries of the $(K_{c}+1)\times(K_{c}+1)$ matrix $V^{T}V$ . To do so, we first establish several properties of $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ . In Lemma II.4, we show that $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ is negative for half of all bitstrings $z$ . Lemma II.5 then characterizes the product $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)$ . These results let us evaluate entries of $V^{T}V$ , which take the form $\sum_{z,n}p^{(n)}_{0}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ and $\sum_{z,n}\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)$ . Finally, in Theorem II.7, we show that $V^{T}V$ , and hence our estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)$ , can be constructed efficiently.

#### Lemma II.4.

Assuming $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ $\neq 0$ , the number of bitstrings $z$ where $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ is negative $|\{z\;|\;\sgn(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z))=-1\}|=2^{N-1}$ .

Proof— Recall that $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=2\im\big[\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}(C^{(n)}_{1})^{\dagger}\cdots(C^{(n)}_{t})^{\dagger}P_{\alpha}C^{(n)}_{t}\cdots C^{(n)}_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}\big]$ . Now, we first analyze the sign of the $\im[]$ term. Now, let $(C^{(n)}_{1})^{\dagger}\cdots(C^{(n)}_{t})^{\dagger}P_{\alpha}C^{(n)}_{t}\cdots C^{(n)}_{1}=\phi P^{\prime}_{\alpha}$ , where $\phi=\pm 1$ . We want to examine the sign of

$$ \displaystyle\phi\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}P^{\prime}_{\alpha}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}. $$

By Theorem II.5, we know if $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\neq 0$ , then this is precisely the sign of $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ .

To proceed, let $a=a_{1}\cdots a_{N}$ be a bitstring defined as follows:

$$ \displaystyle a_{i}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }(P^{\prime}_{\alpha})_{i}\in\{X,Y\}\\
0,&\text{if }(P^{\prime}_{\alpha})_{i}\in\{Z,I\}.\end{cases} $$

In other words, $a$ is a bitstring denoting the positions where $P^{\prime}_{\alpha}$ is either $X$ or $Y$ . From examining Eq. (II.27), it is straightforward the see that $\sgn(\phi\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}P^{\prime}_{\alpha}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z})=\sgn(\phi(-1)^{n_{z,a}}i^{n_{y}})$ , where $n_{z,a}=\text{wt}(z\odot a)$ and $n_{y}$ is the number of Pauli $Y$ in $P^{\prime}_{\alpha}$ . As $\phi$ and $i^{n_{y}}$ are constant across all bitstrings $z$ , we just need to show that $(-1)^{n_{z,a}}$ is negative on $2^{N-1}$ bitstrings and positive on the other $2^{N-1}$ bitstrings in order to prove our statement. This is precisely shown in Lemma I.2. ∎

From our above discussion, we can also conclude the following formula,

$$ \displaystyle\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=\frac{\im[\phi(-1)^{n_{z,a}}i^{n_{y}}]}{2^{N-1}}, $$

where the definitions of $\phi$ , $n_{z,a}$ , and $n_{y}$ can be found in the above Lemma. Now, we establish some more properties of $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ that allow us to analyze the entries of $V^{T}V$ .

#### Lemma II.5.

Consider

$$ \displaystyle\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle=2\im\big[\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}(C^{(n)}_{1})^{\dagger}\cdots(C^{(n)}_{t})^{\dagger}P_{\alpha}C^{(n)}_{t}\cdots C^{(n)}_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}\big] \displaystyle=2\im[\phi\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}P^{\prime}_{\alpha}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}] $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z) \displaystyle=2\im\big[\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}(C^{(n)}_{1})^{\dagger}\cdots(C^{(n)}_{t^{\prime}})^{\dagger}P_{\beta}C^{(n)}_{t^{\prime}}\cdots C^{(n)}_{1}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}\big] \displaystyle=2\im[\varphi\bra{z}\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}P^{\prime}_{\beta}\ket{0}\braket{0|\mathrm{H}^{\otimes N}|z}], $$

where $\phi,\varphi\in[\pm 1]$ and $(C^{(n)}_{1})^{\dagger}\cdots(C^{(n)}_{t(t^{\prime})})^{\dagger}P_{\alpha(\beta)}C^{(n)}_{t(t^{\prime})}\cdots C^{(n)}_{1}=\phi(\varphi)\times P^{\prime}_{\alpha(\beta)}$ . Let $a$ be the bitstring indicating the positions of $X$ and $Y$ in $P^{\prime}_{\alpha}$ , and $a^{\prime}$ analogously for $P_{\beta}$ (Eq. (II.28)). Finally let $n_{y}(n^{\prime}_{y})$ be the number of Pauli $Y$ s in $P_{\alpha(\beta)}$ . The number of bitstrings $z$ where $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)$ is negative is

$$ \displaystyle|\{z\;|\;\sgn(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z))=-1\}|=\begin{cases}2^{N-1}&\text{when }a\neq a^{\prime},\\
0&\text{when }a=a^{\prime}\text{ and }\sgn(i^{n_{y}}\phi)=\sgn(i^{n^{\prime}_{y}}\varphi)\\
2^{N},&\text{when }a=a^{\prime}\text{ and }\sgn(i^{n_{y}}\phi)=-\sgn(i^{n^{\prime}_{y}}\varphi).\end{cases} $$

Proof— We first consider the case when $a\neq a^{\prime}$ . By the logic of Lemma II.4, $\sgn(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z))$ is determined by $\phi\varphi(-1)^{n_{z,a}+n_{z,a^{\prime}}}i^{n_{y}+n^{\prime}_{y}}$ , where $n_{z,a}=\text{wt}(z\odot a)$ . Now, as $i^{n_{y}+n^{\prime}_{y}}\phi\varphi$ is constant across all bitstrings, we just need to show that $(-1)^{n_{z,a}+n_{z,a^{\prime}}}$ switches sign on half of all bitstrings. Indeed, by Lemma I.3, if $a\neq a^{\prime}$ , $\sgn((-1)^{n_{z,a}+n_{z,a^{\prime}}})=-1$ on $2^{N-1}$ bitstrings and $=1$ on the rest.

We now consider when $a=a^{\prime}$ and $\sgn(i^{n_{y}}\phi)=\sgn(i^{n^{\prime}_{y}}\varphi)$ . This means that $n_{z,a}=n_{z,a^{\prime}}$ . So, $\sgn(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z))$ is determined by $\phi\varphi(-1)^{2n_{z,a}}i^{n_{y}+n^{\prime}_{y}}=i^{n_{y}+n^{\prime}_{y}}\phi\varphi$ . By assumption, $\sgn(i^{n_{y}}\phi)=\sgn(i^{n^{\prime}_{y}}\varphi)$ , so $\sgn(i^{n_{y}+n^{\prime}_{y}}\phi\varphi)$ $=1$ . Thus, $\sgn(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z))=1$ for all bitstrings.

Finally, we consider when $a=a^{\prime}$ and $\sgn(i^{n_{y}}\phi)=-\sgn(i^{n^{\prime}_{y}}\varphi)$ . As before, $\sgn(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z))$ is determined by $i^{n_{y}+n^{\prime}_{y}}\phi\varphi$ in this case. By our assumption, $\sgn(i^{n_{y}+n^{\prime}_{y}}\phi\varphi)=-1$ . Thus, $\sgn(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z))=-1$ for all bitstrings. ∎

Using the above results, we can now explicitly compute $V^{T}V$ , and thereby our estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)$ (Eq. (II.26)), in a computationally efficient manner. This is established in the Theorem below.

#### Theorem II.7.

The classical complexity of computing $\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)$ (Eq. (II.26)) is $O(n_{c}K_{c}N^{2}+n_{c}K_{c}^{2}N+K^{3}_{c}+K_{c}NM)$ .

Proof— We first need to compute $\phi$ , $a$ , and $n_{y}$ for each of the $n_{c}K_{c}$ perturbations $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ , as defined in Lemma II.5. This involves evolving a Pauli string by a Clifford in the stabilizer formalism, which takes $O(N^{2})$ time, for a total cost of $O(n_{c}K_{c}N^{2})$ .

We then compute the entries of $V^{T}V$ . Now, $(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t}$ = $\sum_{\tilde{z}}p^{all}_{0}(\tilde{z})\delta p^{all}_{\alpha,t}(\tilde{z})=\sum_{n,z}p^{(n)}_{0}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=0$ deterministically by Lemma II.4. Meanwhile, $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t,\beta t^{\prime}}=\sum_{\tilde{z}}\delta p^{all}_{\alpha,t}(\tilde{z})\delta p^{all}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(\tilde{z})=\sum_{n,z}\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)$ . Now, $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)$ has magnitude $\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}$ for every bitstring $z$ , with sign given by $\sgn(\phi(-1)^{n_{z,a}}i^{n_{y}})$ . Thus, by Lemma II.5

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{z}\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p^{(n)}_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(z)=\begin{cases}0&\text{when }a\neq a^{\prime}\\
\frac{1}{2^{N-2}},&\text{when }a=a^{\prime}\text{ and }\sgn(i^{n_{y}}\phi)=\sgn(i^{n^{\prime}_{y}}\varphi)\\
-\frac{1}{2^{N-2}},&\text{when }a=a^{\prime}\text{ and }\sgn(i^{n_{y}}\phi)=-\sgn(i^{n^{\prime}_{y}}\varphi).\end{cases} $$

Computing this for each of $(K_{c}+1)^{2}$ pairs costs $O(n_{c}(K_{c}+1)^{2}N)$ . We note that this implies that $V^{T}V$ is approximately diagonal, only having off-diagonal terms where the transformed Pauli strings corresponding to signals $\alpha,t$ and $\beta,t^{\prime}$ have Pauli operators $X$ and $Y$ at the exact same positions.

We then invert $V^{T}V$ , which generally costs $O((K_{c}+1)^{3})$ . We must also calculate $V^{T}_{i,\tilde{z}}\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}$ for all $K_{c}+1$ rows $i$ and every sample we measure. This can be done using the formula $\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha,t}(z)=\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}\im[\phi(-1)^{n_{z,a}}i^{n_{y}}]$ , which costs $O(K_{c}NM)$ . ∎

#### II.1.2 Invertibility

Before we analyze the sample complexity of our estimators, we first highlight some important conclusions from our preceding analysis. Specifically, we justify why we expect $V^{T}V$ to be invertible, even with exponentially many signals.

First, we have calculated the entries of $V^{T}V$ for both incoherent and coherent signals, where the matrix $V$ is defined above Eq. (II.20) for incoherent signals and above Eq. (II.26) for coherent signals. Now, in both cases, our results show that $V^{T}V$ is approximately a diagonal matrix.

Specifically, for incoherent signals, the entries of $V^{T}V$ are given by:

$$ \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{0,0} \displaystyle=\sum_{n,z}(p_{0}^{(n)}(z))^{2}=n_{c}, \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{0,\beta t} \displaystyle=\sum_{n,z}p_{0}^{(n)}(z)k_{\beta,t}^{(n)}(z)\approx 0, \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t^{\prime},\beta t} \displaystyle=\sum_{n,z}k_{\alpha,t^{\prime}}^{(n)}(z)k_{\beta,t}^{(n)}(z)\approx n_{c}\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\delta_{t,t^{\prime}}. $$

In all entries, $n$ runs from $1$ to $n_{c}$ and $z$ across all $2^{N}$ bitstrings. In the first equation, we have used the fact that $p_{0}^{(n)}(z)=\delta_{z,0}$ . In the second, we note that each $(V^{T}V)_{0,\beta t}$ is only nonzero if the signal $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ maps exactly to $z=0$ in the sense of Theorem II.1 for any circuit. This happens with exponentially small probability $\frac{n_{c}}{2^{N}}$ , so we approximate $(V^{T}V)_{0,\beta t}\approx 0$ . Similarly, in the third equation, when $\gamma_{\alpha}(t^{\prime})=\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ , then $k_{\alpha,t^{\prime}}^{(n)}(z)=k_{\beta.t}^{(n)}(z)$ are both probability distributions supported on a single bitstring, and $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t^{\prime},\beta t}=n_{c}$ . Otherwise, when $\gamma_{\alpha}(t^{\prime})\neq\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ , $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t^{\prime},\beta t}=0$ with exponentially high probability for the same reason as the second equation.

For coherent signals, the entries of $V^{T}V$ are given by

$$ \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{0,0} \displaystyle=\sum_{n,z}(\underbrace{p_{0}^{(n)}(z))^{2}}_{=\frac{1}{2^{2N}}}=\frac{n_{c}}{2^{N}}, \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t} \displaystyle=\sum_{n,z}p_{0}^{(n)}(z)\delta p_{\alpha,t}^{(n)}(z)=0, \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t^{\prime},\beta t} \displaystyle=\sum_{n,z}\delta p_{\alpha,t}^{(n)}(z)\delta p_{\beta,t^{\prime}}^{(n)}(z)\approx\frac{n_{c}}{2^{N-1}}\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\delta_{t,t^{\prime}}. $$

In the first equation, we have used the fact that for coherent signals, $p_{0}^{(n)}(z)$ is the uniform distribution overall bitstrings $z$ . In the second, we note that each $(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t}$ is zero by Lemma (II.27). In the third, when $\theta_{\alpha}(t^{\prime})=\theta_{\beta}(t)$ , then $\sum_{z}\delta p_{\alpha,t}^{(n)}(z)\delta p_{\beta,t^{\prime}}^{(n)}(z)=\frac{1}{2^{N-2}}$ by Theorem II.7. Thus, using the fact that approximately $\frac{n_{c}}{2}$ $\delta p_{\alpha,t}^{(n)}(z)$ are nonzero over all circuits, $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t,\alpha t}=\frac{n_{c}}{2}\frac{1}{2^{N-2}}$ . Otherwise, when $\theta_{\alpha}(t^{\prime})\neq\theta_{\beta}(t)$ , $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t^{\prime},\beta t}$ is only nonzero when two random Pauli strings corresponding to the two signals have $X$ and $Y$ operators in the exact same qubit positions (see Theorem II.7). This happens with exponentially small probability $\frac{n_{c}}{2^{N}}$ over all circuits, so we approximate $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t^{\prime},\beta t}\approx 0$ . Moreover, if an off-diagonal entry is indeed nonzero, its magnitude would be $a\frac{1}{2^{N-2}}$ , where $a$ is the number of circuits in which two different signals happened to collide—this is, on average, much less than $\frac{n_{c}}{2}$ .

Overall, we see that for both types of signal, $V^{T}V$ is approximately diagonal, with sparse, randomly distributed off-diagonal entries of smaller magnitude. As long as the diagonal entries are bounded away from zero (which we achieve in the coherent case with a sufficiently large $n_{c}$ ), we expect $V^{T}V$ to be invertible [8]. This justifies the use of least-squares linear regression (expressions Eq. (II.20) and (II.26)) for our estimators, which requires that the columns of $V$ are linearly independent and hence $V^{T}V$ is invertible.

#### II.1.3 Typical sample complexity

We now compute the variances $\textrm{Var}(\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t))$ and $\textrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t))$ , with results given in Eq. (II.44) and Eq. (II.48) and stated in Property 5.

Incoherent Signals— $V^{T}V$ , as defined above in Eq. (II.20), is approximately a diagonal matrix, with off-diagonal entries nonzero only when two signals map to the same bitstring in a circuit, in the sense of Theorem II.1. Thus, for our calculation here, we approximate $V^{T}V=\text{diag}(\frac{1}{n_{c}},\cdots,\frac{1}{n_{c}})$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle v_{ic,0}=\frac{1}{n_{c}}\sum_{z,n}p_{0}^{(n)}(z)\frac{\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}}{M/n_{c}}=\sum_{\tilde{z}}p_{0}^{all}(\tilde{z})\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M},\;\;v_{ic,\beta t}=\frac{1}{n_{c}}\sum_{z,n}k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z)\frac{\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}}{M/n_{c}}=\sum_{z}k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(\tilde{z})\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M}, $$

where $\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}$ are the counts for bitstring $z$ measured for the $n$ th circuit and $\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}$ is defined in Eq. (II.21). We can use Eq. (I.93) to calculate the variance of this, along with some modifications:

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Var}(v_{ic,\beta t}) \displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{z,n}(k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z))^{2}\frac{p^{(n)}(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})}{n_{c}} \displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{M}A\underbrace{\sum_{z,n}(k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z))^{2}\frac{p^{(n)}_{0}(z)}{n_{c}}}_{=0}+\frac{1}{M}A\underbrace{\sum_{z,n}(k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z))^{2}\sum_{\alpha t^{\prime}}\frac{k^{(n)}_{\alpha t^{\prime}}}{n_{c}}(z)}_{=\delta_{\alpha t^{\prime},\beta t}}\frac{\gamma_{\alpha}(t^{\prime})}{1-\gamma_{\alpha}(t^{\prime})} \displaystyle=\frac{A}{M}\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}. $$

In the first line, we must consider $\frac{p^{(n)}(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})}{n_{c}}$ as this is a properly normalized probability distribution: $\sum_{z,n}\frac{p^{(n)}(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})}{n_{c}}=1$ . Moreover, $\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}$ can be considered to be drawn from the distribution $\frac{p^{all}(\tilde{z}|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})}{n_{c}}$ with $M$ samples. We also drop higher-order terms in $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ . In the second line, we replaced $p^{(n)}(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})$ with Eq. (II.15) and used the approximation that each signal maps to a unique bitstring for every circuit.

Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Var}(\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t))=\textrm{Var}\bigg(\frac{v_{ic,\beta t}}{v_{ic,0}+v_{ic,\beta t}}\bigg) \displaystyle\approx\frac{\textrm{Var}(v_{ic,\beta t})}{(A+\frac{A\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)})^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{A}{M}\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}\times\bigg(\frac{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{A}\bigg)^{2} \displaystyle\approx\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{AM}. $$

In the first line, we have used Eq. (I.19) and dropped higher-order terms in $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ . We also drop higher-order terms in the last line.

Coherent Signals— $V^{T}V$ here, as defined above Eq. (II.26), is also approximately a diagonal matrix: an off-diagonal term is only nonzero when the second or third conditions of Eq. (II.31) are satisfied. This happens if two random Pauli strings happen to have $X$ and $Y$ operators in the exact same qubit positions, which occurs with exponentially small probability. Thus, we approximate $V^{T}V=\text{diag}(\frac{2^{N}}{n_{c}},\frac{2}{n_{c}}2^{N-2},\cdots,\frac{2}{n_{c}}2^{N-2})$ , where we use the fact that approximately $\frac{n_{c}}{2}$ $\delta p^{n}_{\alpha t}(z)$ are nonzero over all circuits. Then,

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)=\frac{2^{N-1}}{\hat{A}n_{c}}\sum_{z,n}\delta p^{n}_{\alpha t}(z)\frac{\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}}{M/n_{c}}=\frac{2^{N-1}}{\hat{A}}\sum_{\tilde{z}}\delta p^{all}_{\alpha t}(z)\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M}, $$

where $\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}$ is the number of times bitstring $z$ is measured for circuit $n$ , and $\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}$ is defined in Eq. (II.21). As before, $\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}$ can be considered to be drawn from the distribution $\frac{p^{all}(\tilde{z}|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})}{n_{c}}$ with $M$ samples. Now,

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)) \displaystyle\approx\frac{2^{2N-2}}{MA^{2}}\sum_{z,n}(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha t}(z))^{2}\frac{p^{(n)}(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})}{n_{c}} \displaystyle\approx\frac{2^{2N-2}}{MA^{2}}\underbrace{\sum_{z,n}(\delta p^{(n)}_{\alpha t}(z))^{2}\frac{p^{(n)}_{0}(z)}{n_{c}}}_{=\frac{2^{N}n_{c}}{2}\times\frac{1}{2^{2N-2}}\times\frac{1}{2^{N}n_{c}}=\frac{1}{2^{2N-1}}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2MA^{2}}. $$

As before, we used Eqs. (I.19) and (I.93) while ignoring higher-order terms in $\theta_{\alpha}$ .

#### II.1.4 Bounds on sample complexity for worst-case error

We can also bound the worst-case errors of our estimators $\max_{\beta,t}|\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)-\gamma_{\beta}(t)|$ (given in Theorem II.8) and $\max_{\alpha,t}|\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)-\theta_{\alpha}(t)|$ (given in Theorem II.9), thereby justifying Property 6. The proofs of Theorems II.8 and II.9 proceed by applying sub-exponential tail bounds of the Poisson distribution, which can be related to the multinomial statistics of the measured bitstrings, in order to constrain the error of our estimators.

#### Theorem II.8.

Assume the perturbative regime of small signals, such that $A$ (defined in Eq. (II.16)) is $O(1)$ , and neglect bias. In the presence of $K_{ic}$ total incoherent signals $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ , a precision $\max_{\beta,t}|\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)-\gamma_{\beta}(t)|\leq\epsilon$ for small $\epsilon$ can be achieved with probability $1-\delta$ by taking $M=O(\max\{\frac{\log(\frac{K_{ic}}{\delta})}{\epsilon^{2}},\frac{\log(\frac{K_{ic}}{\delta})}{\epsilon},\frac{\log(\frac{K_{ic}^{2}}{\delta})\log(\frac{1}{\delta})}{N}\})$ , with the first term being dominant for small enough $\epsilon$ .

Proof. We want to bound the error of our estimator Eq. (II.20). First, we take $n_{c}=O(\frac{K^{2}_{ic}}{\delta^{\prime}}/N)$ large enough such that with high probability $1-\delta^{\prime}$ , the protocol succeeds (Theorem II.3). We can rewrite our estimator as

$$ \displaystyle v_{{ic},l}=\sum_{z,n}w_{l,z^{(n)}}\frac{\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}}{M/n_{c}},\;\;\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)=\frac{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}+v_{{ic},{0}}}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle w_{l,z^{(n)}}=\sum_{i}(V^{T}V)_{l,i}V^{T}_{i,z^{(n)}}, $$

and $z^{(n)}$ indicates bitstring $z$ drawn from the $n$ th circuit. We further denote $\mathbb{E}(v_{{ic},l})=\bar{v}_{{ic},l}$ .

Now, $\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}\sim\text{Multinomial}(M/n_{c},p^{(n)}(z))$ , where we take $M/n_{c}$ samples deterministically. We can consider an alternative process whereby $X\sim\text{Poisson}(M/n_{c})$ samples are taken for each circuit, such that $\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}\sim\text{Poisson}(Mp^{(n)}(z)/n_{c})$ [7]. In this case, $\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}$ for different $z$ , $n$ , are independent random variables. By Lemma I.6, analyzing our procedure in this way incurs at most a constant error in the sample complexity. We therefore proceed by treating our variables as Poisson.

After Poissonization, $w_{l,z^{(n)}}\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}$ is a sub-exponential random variable with parameters $\nu^{2}=w^{2}_{l,z^{(n)}}ep^{(n)}(z)\frac{M}{n_{c}}$ and $\alpha=|w_{l,z^{(n)}}|$ (see Lemma I.5 and Corollary I.2.1). Using the fact that summations of independent sub-exponential random variables are also sub-exponential, $\sum_{z,n}w_{l,z^{(n)}}\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}$ is sub-exponential with effective $\nu_{l}^{2}=\sum_{z,n}w^{2}_{l,z^{(n)}}ep^{(n)}(z)\frac{M}{n_{c}}$ and $\alpha_{l}=\max_{z,n}|w_{l,z^{(n)}}|$ [1].

Let us now consider the cases $l=0$ and $l=\beta t$ seperately. By the discussion in Section II.1.3, $w_{\beta t,z^{(n)}}\approx\frac{1}{n_{c}}k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z)$ , where $k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z)$ is defined for a fixed circuit $n$ in Eq. (II.12). Similarly, $w_{\beta t,z^{(n)}}\approx\frac{1}{n_{c}}p^{0}_{n}(z)$ . Recall that $p^{0}_{n}(z)$ is deterministic, $p^{0}_{n}(0)=1$ . By Theorem II.1, $k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z)$ is also deterministic: for each $n$ , $k^{(n)}_{\beta t}(z^{*})=1$ for some $z^{*}$ . Using this information, we see that $\nu_{\beta t}^{2}\approx\frac{eM}{n^{3}_{c}}\sum_{n}\gamma_{\beta}(t)=\frac{eM\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{n^{2}_{c}}$ and ${\nu_{0}}^{2}\approx\frac{eMA}{n^{2}_{c}}$ , where $A$ is defined in Eq. (II.16). Thus, we can write

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{l}^{2}=\frac{M\mathcal{C}_{l}}{n^{2}_{c}},\,\,\alpha_{l}=\frac{\mathcal{A}_{l}}{n_{c}}, $$

where $\mathcal{C}_{l}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{l}$ are $O(1)$ constants. Using sub-exponential tail bounds,

$$ \displaystyle\text{Pr}\bigg(\bigg|\sum_{z,n}w_{\beta t,z^{(n)}}\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}-\sum_{z}w_{\beta t,z^{(n)}}\frac{M}{n_{c}}p^{(n)}(z)\bigg|\geq\epsilon\bigg) \displaystyle\leq 2\exp\bigg(-\min\bigg\{\frac{n^{2}_{c}\epsilon^{2}}{2M\mathcal{C}_{\beta t}},\frac{n_{c}\epsilon}{2\mathcal{A}_{\beta t}}\bigg\}\bigg), \displaystyle\text{Pr}\bigg(\bigg|\sum_{z,n}w_{0,z^{(n)}}\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}-\sum_{z}w_{0,z^{(n)}}\frac{M}{n_{c}}p^{(n)}(z)\bigg|\geq\epsilon\bigg) \displaystyle\leq 2\exp\bigg(-\min\bigg\{\frac{n^{2}_{c}\epsilon^{2}}{2M\mathcal{C}_{0}},\frac{n_{c}\epsilon}{2\mathcal{A}_{0}}\bigg\}\bigg). $$

These bounds imply

$$ \displaystyle\text{Pr}(|v_{ic,{\beta t}}-\bar{v}_{ic,{\beta t}}|\geq\epsilon)=\text{Pr}\bigg(\bigg|\sum_{z,n}w_{\beta t,z^{(n)}}\frac{\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}}{M/n_{c}}-\sum_{z}w_{\beta t,z^{(n)}}p^{(n)}(z)\bigg|\geq\epsilon\bigg) \displaystyle\leq 2\exp\bigg(-\min\bigg\{\frac{M\epsilon^{2}}{2\mathcal{C}_{\beta t}},\frac{M\epsilon}{2\mathcal{A}_{\beta t}}\bigg\}\bigg), \displaystyle\text{Pr}(|v_{ic,{0}}-\bar{v}_{ic,{0}}|\geq\epsilon)=\text{Pr}\bigg(\bigg|\sum_{z,n}w_{0,z^{(n)}}\frac{\hat{N}_{z^{(n)}}}{M/n_{c}}-\sum_{z}w_{0,z^{(n)}}p^{(n)}(z)\bigg|\geq\epsilon\bigg) \displaystyle\leq 2\exp\bigg(-\min\bigg\{\frac{M\epsilon^{2}}{2\mathcal{C}_{0}},\frac{M\epsilon}{2\mathcal{A}_{0}}\bigg\}\bigg). $$

We note that the Gaussian-like tail $e^{-\epsilon^{2}}$ occurs for small deviations about the mean, $\epsilon\leq\frac{\mathcal{C}_{l}}{\mathcal{A}_{l}}$ .

Now, we further want to bound

$$ \displaystyle\bigg|\frac{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}+v_{{ic},{0}}}-\frac{\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}+\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}}}\bigg|=|\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)-\gamma_{\beta}(t)|. $$

First, we work in a regime where $|v_{{ic},{0}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}}|\leq r$ and $|v_{{ic},{\beta t}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}|\leq r^{\prime}$ for some chosen $r,r^{\prime}<1$ . By Eqs. (II.54) and (II.55), this can be achieved with probability $1-\delta_{1}-\delta_{2}$ by taking

$$ \displaystyle M\geq\max\bigg\{\frac{2\log(2/\delta_{1})\mathcal{C}_{0}}{r^{2}},\frac{2\log(2/\delta_{1})\mathcal{A}_{0}}{r},\frac{2\log(2/\delta_{2})\mathcal{C}_{\beta t}}{r^{\prime 2}},\frac{2\log(2/\delta_{2})\mathcal{A}_{\beta t}}{r^{\prime}}\bigg\}. $$

Now, we have chosen $r$ and $r^{\prime}$ sufficiently small so that we can Taylor expand $\frac{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}+v_{{ic},{0}}}$ about its mean:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}+v_{{ic},{0}}}-\frac{\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}+\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}}}=\frac{\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}}}{(\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}+\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}})^{2}}(v_{{ic},{\beta t}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}})-\frac{\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{(\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}+\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}})^{2}}(v_{{ic},{0}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}})+d. $$

$d$ is the error of the Taylor expansion, which can be quantified by Taylor’s Remainder Theorem,

$$ \displaystyle d=-\frac{v_{1}}{(v_{1}+v_{2})^{3}}(v_{{ic},{\beta t}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}})^{2}+\frac{v_{2}}{(v_{1}+v_{2})^{3}}(v_{{ic},{0}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}})^{2}+\frac{v_{2}-v_{1}}{(v_{1}+v_{2})^{3}}(v_{{ic},{\beta t}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}})(v_{{ic},{0}}-\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}}). $$

The coefficients originate from the second-order derivatives of $\frac{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}}{v_{{ic},{\beta t}}+v_{{ic},{0}}}$ evaluated at some point $v_{1}\in[v_{{ic},{0}},\bar{v}_{{ic},{0}}]$ and $v_{2}\in[v_{{ic},{\beta t}},\bar{v}_{{ic},{\beta t}}]$ . #### II.1.5 Strong robustness of the incoherent signal protocol

As discussed in the main text and in Property 7, classical error correction techniques can be used to error-correct our estimator $\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)$ in the presence of readout error. Here, we show that our incoherent sensing protocol is correctable for large enough $N$ scaling with $\log K_{ic}^{2}$ .

By Theorem II.1, each signal $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ is mapped to a single bitstring. We thus denote the set of bitstrings which are in correspondence with the set of signals for the $n$ th circuit as $\mathcal{Z}_{n}=\{z|k^{(n)}_{\beta}(z)=1\}$ . For each circuit $n$ , readout error occurs when we measure a bitstring $z\notin\mathcal{Z}_{n}$ .

Let $d_{min}(\mathcal{Z}_{n})$ be the minimum pairwise Hamming distance between bitstrings in $\mathcal{Z}_{n}$ . If the closest Hamming distance between the measured bitstring $z$ and and any bitstring in $\mathcal{Z}_{n}$ is $d_{H}(z,\mathcal{Z}_{n})\leq\frac{d_{min}(\mathcal{Z}_{n})}{2}$ , then we can correct $z$ by simply replacing it with the closest bitstring in $\mathcal{Z}_{n}$ in Hamming distance. We call compatibility with active error correction as strongly robust against readout error. We note that as our Clifford circuits are randomly selected, the random encoding of signals to bitstrings is inherent in our protocol. We can bound the probability that for a given random encoding, $\mathcal{Z}_{n}$ achieves $d_{min}(\mathcal{Z}_{n})\geq d$ , where $d$ is the desired minimum distance between codewords. The result is given in Theorem II.10.

#### Theorem II.10.

For randomly selected Clifford circuits $\{C_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ , and $k_{\alpha,t}(z)$ defined in Eq. (II.12), the probability

$$ \displaystyle\text{Pr}(d_{min}(\mathcal{Z})\geq d)\geq\frac{\prod_{m=0}^{K_{ic}-1}(2^{N}-mV(N,d-1))}{(2^{N})^{K_{ic}}}, $$

where $\mathcal{Z}=\{z|k_{\alpha,t}(z)=1\}$ , $d_{min}(\mathcal{Z})$ is the minimum pairwise Hamming distance between bitstrings in $\mathcal{Z}$ , $K_{ic}$ is the total number of $k_{\alpha,t}(z)$ , and $V(N,d-1)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\begin{pmatrix}N\\ j\end{pmatrix}$ is the volume of a ball with radius $d-1$ .

Proof. We can think of this problem as randomly choosing $K_{ic}$ bitstrings to form $\mathcal{Z}$ , and determining the probability $\text{Pr}(d_{min}(\mathcal{Z})\geq d)$ . We calculate this by counting the number of valid bitstrings in $\{0,1\}^{N}$ .

For the first selected bitstring $z^{*}$ , there are no constraints, and the probability of choosing a valid bitstring is $\frac{2^{N}}{2^{N}}=1$ . For the second selected bitstring, we cannot choose any bitstrings $z$ s.t. $d_{H}(z,z^{*})\leq d-1$ . This excludes $V(N,d-1)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\begin{pmatrix}N\\ j\end{pmatrix}$ possible choices, leading to a probability of valid selection of $\frac{2^{N}-V(N,d-1)}{2^{N}}$ . We repeat this $K_{ic}$ times, leading to $\text{Pr}(d_{min}(\mathcal{Z})\geq d)\geq\frac{\prod_{m=0}^{K_{ic}-1}(2^{N}-mV(N,d-1))}{(2^{N})^{K_{ic}}}$ . ∎

Now, we note that $V(N,d-1)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\begin{pmatrix}N\\ j\end{pmatrix}\leq 2^{NH(\frac{d-1}{N})}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle H(x)=-x\log_{2}(x)-(1-x)\log_{2}(1-x) $$

is the binary entropy.

Thus, letting $q=2^{-N\big(1-H\big(\frac{d-1}{N}\big)\big)}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{m=0}^{K_{ic}-1}(2^{N}-mV(N,d-1)) \displaystyle\geq\prod_{m=0}^{K_{ic}-1}2^{N}(1-mq) \displaystyle\geq 2^{K_{ic}N}\exp\bigg(-q\sum_{m=0}^{K_{ic}-1}m-q^{2}\sum_{m=0}^{K_{ic}-1}m^{2}\bigg) $$

where we work in the regime of large $N$ and $\frac{d}{N}<1$ , so $q$ is small and $qK_{ic}\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . In the second inequality, we have used the fact that $\ln(1-x^{2})\geq x-x^{2}$ when $0\leq x\leq\frac{1}{2}$ .

Thus, neglecting terms higher-order in $qK_{ic}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\text{Pr}(d_{min}(\mathcal{Z})\geq d)\geq\exp\bigg(-2^{-N\big(1-H\big(\frac{d-1}{N}\big)\big)}\frac{K_{ic}(K_{ic}-1)}{2}\bigg). $$

This decreases exponentially in $K^{2}_{ic}$ , but tends towards $1$ double-exponentially with increasing $N$ . With large enough system size $N\sim\log\big(\frac{K_{ic}^{2}}{\delta}\big)/(1-H(\alpha))$ , we thus expect to achieve $\frac{d_{min}}{N}>\alpha$ with probability $1-\delta$ .

Although strong robustness only applies to our incoherent protocol, we note that Eq. (II.20) can also be used to sense coherent signals quadratically, up to $\theta_{\alpha}(t)^{2}$ . Thus, in a situation where robustness is crucial, the incoherent protocol could be used to detect both $\hat{\gamma}_{\alpha}(t)$ and $\theta_{\alpha}(t)^{2}$ . Once the forms of the nonzero signals are determined, a more targeted sensing procedure can be used to pinpoint the precise magnitude and sign of the coherent signals $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ .

Moreover, even without using active error correction, we expect our estimators to be weakly robust against readout error—readout error will not affect the SQL scaling of our estimators. For our incoherent estimator Eq. (II.20), this is true following the discussion in Section I.1.4 as our random Clifford circuits will generally map signals to high-weight bitstrings (c.f. Theorem II.1), such that they are minimally affected by readout error. For our coherent estimator Eq. (II.26), weak robustness follows from an analogous discussion to Section I.2.4.

#### II.1.6 Thresholding

When our signals are guaranteed to be sparse, we can enforce sparse solutions and improve the performance of our estimators (Eq. (II.20), Eq. (II.26)) in practice by hard thresholding, a type of statistical regularization [5]:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{\alpha,thres}(t)=\begin{cases}\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)&\text{if }|\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)|\geq\theta_{thres}\\
0&\text{if }|\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)|<\theta_{thres}.\end{cases} $$

$\hat{\gamma}_{\beta,thres}(t)$ is defined analogously. When we are given that all significant signals $\theta_{\alpha}(t)\geq\theta_{min}$ , $\gamma_{\beta}(t)\geq\gamma_{min}$ , we can choose $\theta_{thres}$ and $\gamma_{thres}$ based on $\theta_{min}$ and $\gamma_{min}$ . For instance, using the results of Sec. II.1.3, we can set $\theta_{thres}=\theta_{min}-2\times\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}\textrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\alpha})}$ and $\gamma_{thres}=\gamma_{min}-2\times\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\beta}\textrm{Var}(\hat{\gamma}_{\beta})}$ . In this manner, all estimated signals which have magnitude more than two standard deviations lower than the minimum are set to zero. Thresholding is applied for the numerical results shown in the main text. If $\theta_{min}$ and $\gamma_{min}$ are unknown but expected to be nonzero, than we can set $\theta_{thres}$ and $\gamma_{thres}$ to $2\times\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}\textrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\alpha})}$ or $2\times\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\beta}\textrm{Var}(\hat{\gamma}_{\beta})}$ , respectively, thus zeroing signals within two standard deviations of zero.

#### II.1.7 Overlapping signal generators

In our estimators Eqs. (II.20) and (II.26), we assumed for simplicity that incoherent and coherent signals couple to the system via different sets of Pauli operators. However, our results can be easily modified to account for when the same set of generators $\{P_{\alpha}\}$ gives rise to both incoherent $\gamma_{\alpha}$ and coherent $\theta_{\alpha}$ , as is the case in Fig. 3 of the main text. In this case, Eq. (II.15) becomes

$$ \displaystyle p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})\approx A\big(p_{0}(z)+\sum_{\alpha,t}\bigg(\frac{\gamma_{\alpha}}{1-\gamma_{\alpha}}+\theta^{2}_{\alpha}\bigg)k_{\alpha,t}(z)\big), $$

while Eq. (II.24) stays the same. Our estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}$ (Eq. (II.26)) thus doesn’t change, while $\hat{\gamma}_{\alpha}(t)$ becomes

$$ \displaystyle v_{{ic},{\alpha t}}=\sum_{i,\tilde{z}}(V^{T}V)^{-1}_{\alpha t,i}V^{T}_{i,\tilde{z}}\frac{\hat{N}_{\tilde{z}}}{M/n_{c}},\;\;\hat{\gamma}_{\alpha}(t)=\frac{v_{{ic},{\alpha t}}-A\theta_{\alpha}(t)^{2}}{v_{{ic},{\alpha t}}-A\theta_{\alpha}(t)^{2}+v_{{ic},{0}}},\;\;\hat{A}=v_{ic,0}. $$

We can take the values of $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ to be the best estimates $\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)$ we have from the coherent procedure.

The mechanism enabling the detection of incoherent signals is identical to that of the quadratic Ramsey protocol: each signal is mapped to a distinct bitstring, and the rate at which these bitstrings are detected provides an estimator for the signal magnitude. ### II.2 Applications

In this section, we discuss applications of our multiparameter sensing protocol based on global Clifford unitaries to Hamiltonian learning. In particular, we first show how the protocol can be used as a subroutine for time-independent Hamiltonian learning with Heisenberg-limited scaling, as defined in Refs. [9, 10]. We then formalize time-dependent Hamiltonian learning and introduce a simple class of time-dependent Hamiltonians for which our protocol achieves optimal performance.

#### II.2.1 Time-independent Hamiltonian learning

Broadly, time-independent Hamiltonian learning from dynamics addresses the following problem: given an unknown $H$ and the ability to evolve by $e^{-iHt}$ for any $t>0$ , determine $H$ . Algorithms for accomplishing this task generally use the total evolution time $T$ under the Hamiltonian $H$ as the figure of merit. A variety of methods have been proposed to tackle this task, including estimating derivatives of observables [11, 12], reshaping the Hamiltonian to a simpler form [9, 13, 14, 10], and leveraging potential sparsity of the Hamiltonian [15, 13, 10]. Heisenberg-limited Hamiltonian learning is achieved when $T$ scales with the error of estimation $\epsilon$ as $T\sim 1/\epsilon$ [9, 14, 10], in contrast to the standard scaling $1/\epsilon^{2}$ .

Our protocol can be used as a tool to reach the Heisenberg limit in Hamiltonian learning. Suppose the Hamiltonian $H=\sum{h_{\alpha}}P_{\alpha}$ encodes coherent signals, where $P_{\alpha}$ are arbitrary Pauli strings. We can use our coherent multiparameter sensing procedure to determine each $\theta_{\alpha}=h_{\alpha}\tau$ for a given evolution time $\tau$ over one run, by placing the Hamiltonian evolution between layers of Clifford circuits. Using Eq. (II.48), we see that for a certain error $\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\alpha}[(\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}-\theta_{\alpha})^{2}}]=\epsilon^{*}_{\theta}$ , the total evolution time of our procedure $T$ is

$$ \displaystyle T=M\tau\sim\frac{\tau}{(\epsilon^{*}_{\theta})^{2}}. $$

Now, for Hamiltonian learning, we wish to analyze the scaling of $T$ with respect to the error, $\epsilon_{h}$ , of estimating $h_{\alpha}$ . As $\theta_{\alpha}$ = $h_{\alpha}\tau$ , $\epsilon^{*}_{\theta}=\epsilon_{h}\tau$ . So,

$$ \displaystyle T\sim\frac{1}{(\epsilon^{*}_{\theta})^{2}}\frac{\epsilon^{*}_{\theta}}{\epsilon_{h}}\sim\frac{1}{\epsilon_{h}} $$

for fixed $\epsilon_{\theta}^{*}$ . Thus, by fixing the target phase error $\epsilon^{*}_{\theta}$ and increasing the interrogation time $\tau$ , we achieve $T\sim\frac{1}{\epsilon_{h}}$ scaling. However, for sufficiently long evolution times $\tau$ , the accumulated phases $\theta_{\alpha}$ may become large, violating the perturbative regime assumed by our protocol.

This limitation can be addressed by embedding our scheme into a larger algorithm for learning a time-independent Hamiltonian $H$ , which can achieve Heisenberg-limited scaling. Since our procedure is formulated for perturbatively small signals, such an algorithm may employ iterative or adaptive steps to manage Hamiltonians with larger strengths.

One example is hierarchical learning, introduced in Ref. [10], which partitions Hamiltonian amplitudes into $J=\lceil\log(1/\epsilon_{h})\rceil$ levels. At each level $j$ , all terms $h_{\alpha}$ with amplitudes $2^{-(j+1)}<|h_{\alpha}|<2^{-j}$ are estimated to precision $\epsilon_{h}$ using a subroutine such as the procedure described above. Concretely, the protocol estimates the accumulated phases $h_{\alpha}\tau$ to a target error $\epsilon_{\theta}^{*}$ , which includes both bias and statistical error and is determined by the number of measurement samples $M$ . The corresponding amplitude precision is then $\epsilon_{h}=\epsilon_{\theta}^{*}/\tau$ . Moreover, at level $j$ , estimates of all Hamiltonian terms with amplitudes larger than $2^{-j}$ are already available, defining an effective Hamiltonian $H_{j}$ . These larger contributions can therefore be canceled, allowing the protocol to estimate the residual Hamiltonian $H-H_{j}$ at each step. As the remaining amplitudes decrease exponentially with $j$ , this reduction is compensated by increasing the interrogation time to $2^{j}\tau$ , keeping the accumulated phase at a fixed, perturbative scale. Using this approach, our protocol can be straightforwardly applied to estimate successively smaller terms, though a different method may be required to estimate the largest Hamiltonian coefficients, yielding an overall Heisenberg-limited learning strategy.

#### II.2.2 Time-dependent Hamiltonian learning

In conventional time-independent Hamiltonian learning, one assumes access to unitary evolutions $e^{-iHt}$ for a tunable interrogation time $t>0$ . This assumption does not straightforwardly extend to the learning of time-dependent Hamiltonians, where it becomes necessary to specify both the structure of the time dependence and the nature of the available access to the system’s evolution.

Broadly, we distinguish between two models of time-dependent Hamiltonian learning: absolute and relative. In the absolute setting, the Hamiltonian $H(t)$ is defined with respect to an absolute time reference, and each query provides access only to an evolution operator of the form

$$ U(t_{2},t_{1})=\mathcal{T}\exp\!\left(-\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}H(t^{\prime})\,dt^{\prime}\right), $$

where $\mathcal{T}$ denotes time ordering. In contrast, in the relative setting the Hamiltonian can be reset, so that each query yields an evolution

$$ U(t)=\mathcal{T}\exp\!\left(-\int_{0}^{t}H(t^{\prime})\,dt^{\prime}\right). $$

Absolute time-dependent Hamiltonian learning is relevant for sensing applications such as dark-matter detection [16, 17], where one has no control over when a time-dependent signal is encountered. By contrast, relative time-dependent Hamiltonian learning is more appropriate for controlled settings, such as quantum process tomography [18, 19] or experiments probing the response of a system (e.g., a biomolecular mechanism [20]) to a well-defined trigger. In both cases, constraints on the time dependence and the specific estimation task must be specified more precisely, since an unrestricted formulation would require estimating an arbitrary function $H(t)$ , which entails infinitely many parameters.

In this section, we show that our multiparameter estimation protocol is optimal for learning a simple class of relatively time-dependent Hamiltonians, which we define below. Consider the task of learning a time-dependent Hamiltonian for time $0\leq t\leq\tau$ , where the Hamiltonian is piecewise-constant over $n$ intervals of $\frac{\tau}{n}$ . The Hamiltonian takes the form

$$ \displaystyle H(t_{i})=\sum_{\alpha}h_{\alpha,t_{i}}P_{\alpha},\,\,i\in[0,1,\cdots n-1] $$

where $\{P_{\alpha}\}$ are Pauli strings. Moreover, the Hamiltonian satisfies $\sum_{\alpha,i}(h_{\alpha,t_{i}}\frac{\tau}{n})^{2}\ll 1$ , and the total size of the set $|\{P_{\alpha}\}|<2^{N}/n$ , where $N$ is the number of qubits. No other constraints on the weight or locality of the $P_{\alpha}$ are imposed. As in the time-independent Hamiltonian case, we use the total evolution time $T$ as the figure of merit for the learning algorithm. Moreover, we restrict our analysis to ancilla-free algorithms that utilize all available qubit sensors for sensing and perform a complete measurement of the system after each iteration of the protocol.

#### Theorem II.11.

Consider the task of learning a Hamiltonian of the form Eq. (II.99) using an ancilla-free algorithm that employs all available sensor qubits and performs a complete measurement after each iteration. Assume arbitrarily fast control and no decoherence. The lower bound to achieve error $\mathbb{E}_{\alpha,i}(\hat{h}_{\alpha,i}-h_{\alpha,i})^{2}\leq\epsilon^{2}$ is given by $T=\Omega(\frac{n^{2}}{\tau\epsilon^{2}})$ .

Proof. Suppose $H(t_{n})=hZ^{\otimes N}$ , and $H(t_{i\neq n})=0$ . Then, the Hamiltonian is effectively time-independent and given by $H=hZ^{\otimes N}$ acting over the duration $\frac{n-1}{n}\tau\leq t\leq\tau$ . A straightforward Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) calculation yields the bound

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Var}(\hat{h})\geq\frac{n^{2}}{4M\tau^{2}}. $$

Now, the total evolution time is $T=M\tau$ , where we emphasize that the Hamiltonian must be evolved until $t=\tau$ for each iteration in order to sense the term in the last time interval. Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon^{2}\geq\frac{n^{2}}{4(T/\tau)\tau^{2}}\implies T\geq\frac{n^{2}}{4\tau\epsilon^{2}}. $$

As we have shown the existence of a Hamiltonian which requires total evolution time $T\geq\frac{n^{2}}{4\tau\epsilon^{2}}$ to learn, it follows that any algorithm for learning a generic $H$ of the form Eq (II.99) must take at least $T=\Omega(\frac{n^{2}}{\tau\epsilon^{2}})$ in the worst case ∎.

Now, our coherent multiparameter estimation procedure using Clifford circuits can be directly used to learn the time-dependent $H$ . By Eq. (II.48), we can learn $\theta_{\alpha}(t_{i})\equiv h_{\alpha,t_{i}}\frac{\tau}{n}$ with error

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t_{i}))\approx\frac{1}{2MA^{2}}, $$

where $A=\prod_{i,\alpha}\cos^{2}(\theta_{\alpha}(t_{i}))$ . This scaling is demonstrated in Fig. 3(c) of the main text. Thus, the error of estimating the Hamiltonian terms is

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon^{2}\approx\frac{n^{2}}{2A^{2}\tau^{2}M}=\frac{n^{2}}{2A^{2}\tau T}, $$

where we have used $T=M\tau$ . This achieves $T\sim O(\frac{n^{2}}{\tau\epsilon^{2}})$ , which is optimal according to Theorem II.11. It is worthwhile to explore whether a better algorithm can be developed which further optimizes the constant from $\frac{1}{2}$ to $\frac{1}{4}$ .

### II.4 Random unitary circuits

Rather than using random brickwork Clifford circuits, we can take the brickwork layers to be composed of random two-qubit unitaries drawn from the Haar measure (Fig S3(a)). Let $\mathrm{U}=\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T+1}$ indicate the layers of local unitaries applied between signal accumulation of $T$ timesteps. The use of RUCs to learn incoherent signals is studied in depth in Ref. [21]. Here, we define

$$ \displaystyle U_{i}=\big(U^{i}_{12}\otimes U^{i}_{34}\cdots\otimes U^{i}_{N-1,N}\big)\big(U^{i}_{23}\otimes U^{i}_{34}\cdots\otimes U^{i}_{N-1,1}\big), $$

where each $U^{i}_{j,j+1}\sim\text{Haar}(U(4))$ , and $U(4)$ is the unitary group on $4\times 4$ matrices. At the end of the circuit, we measure in the $z-$ basis, without applying the circuit inverse as the last unitary layer. Unlike the Clifford case, we do not need to take multiple sets of circuits, nor do we need the last unitary to be the inverse of the previous layers. Although this results in less structure than the Clifford-circuit protocol, classical simulation here remains difficult regardless of the inverse constraint, so we omit it and analyze the general case. We note that as only two nearest-neighbor layers are used between signal layers to scramble signals, the requisite circuit depth is quite small. We justify why shallow circuits suffice in Sec. II.4.1.

As before, we can consider how the presence of signals affects the output probability distribution $p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})$ . Now, we define

$$ \displaystyle p_{0}(z) \displaystyle\equiv|\braket{z|U_{T+1}\cdots U_{1}|0}|^{2}, \displaystyle\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle\equiv\partial_{\theta_{\alpha}(t)}p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})=-i\braket{z|\cdots U_{t+1}P_{\alpha}U_{t}\cdots|0}\braket{0|U^{\dagger}_{1}\cdots U^{\dagger}_{T+1}|z}+h.c., \displaystyle k_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle\equiv\partial_{\gamma_{\alpha}(t)}p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})=|\braket{z|\cdots U_{t+1}P_{\alpha}U_{t}\cdots|0}|^{2}, $$

where $P_{\alpha}$ is a Pauli operator that generates the signal.

We can then approximate

$$ \displaystyle p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})\approx A\bigg(p_{0}(z)+\sum_{\alpha,t}\theta_{\alpha}(t)\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z)+\sum_{\beta,t}\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}k_{\beta,t}(z)\bigg), $$

where $A=\prod_{\alpha,t}\cos^{2}(\theta_{\alpha}(t))\prod_{\beta,t^{\prime}}(1-\gamma_{\beta}(t^{\prime}))$ is the probability that no signal occurs. Here, we also assume coherent and incoherent signals couple to the system via different operators $\{P_{\alpha}\}$ , $\{P_{\beta}\}$ for simplicity, but our analysis can be easily extended to when they are present with the same Pauli generators (see Section II.1.7). Now, as before, our estimators are constructed by inverting Eq. (II.108) using linear regression.

Specifically, we think of $p_{0}(z)$ , $\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z)$ , and $k_{\beta,t}(z)$ as vectors over $2^{N}$ bitstrings. We can concatenate them horizontally into a $2^{N}\times(K_{c}+K_{ic}+1)$ dimensional matrix $V$ , with columns $V_{z,0}=p_{0}(z)$ , $V_{z,\alpha}=\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z)$ , and $V_{z,\beta}=k_{\beta,t}(z)$ . We can then rewrite Eq. (II.108) as

$$ \displaystyle p(z|\vec{\theta},\vec{\gamma})\approx A\bigg(V_{z,0}+\sum_{\alpha,t}\theta_{\alpha}(t)V_{z,\alpha}+\sum_{\beta,t}\frac{\gamma_{\beta}(t)}{1-\gamma_{\beta}(t)}V_{z,\beta}\bigg). $$

Defining

$$ \displaystyle v_{l}=\sum_{i,z}(V^{T}V)^{-1}_{l,i}V^{T}_{i,z}\frac{\hat{N}_{z}}{M}, $$

where $\hat{N}_{z}$ is the number of times bitstring $z$ is observed and $M$ is the total number of samples, we then have

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t)=\frac{v_{\alpha}}{v_{0}},\;\;\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t)=\frac{v_{\beta}}{v_{0}+v_{\beta}}. $$

These estimators are unbiased up to higher-order corrections in the signals. We expect these estimators to have sample complexity

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\alpha}(t))=\frac{\beta_{1}}{A^{2}M},\;\;\textrm{Var}(\hat{\gamma}_{\beta}(t))=\frac{\beta_{2}}{A^{2}M}, $$

where $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ are $O(1)$ constants. By the same logic as in Section I.2.4, we also expect these estimators to be weakly robust to readout error.

Numerical results of this procedure are shown in Fig. S4(c),(d). Though our estimators Eq. (II.111) do not perform as well as in the global Clifford or local Clifford case—namely, the scaling of RMS error with $M$ is worse by a constant factor—we still observe SQL scaling, even in the presence of nonzero readout error. Moreover, sparse signals are faithfully reconstructed.

For a more detailed treatment of incoherent signal estimation using RUCs, we refer the reader to Ref. [21], which considers this problem in the context of benchmarking and derives provably optimal estimators.

#### II.4.1 Invertibility

Here, we show through random matrix calculations why we expect $V^{T}V$ to be invertible when using local random unitary circuits.

To be clear, we first write the following expressions for the entries of $V^{T}V$ :

$$ \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{0,0} \displaystyle=\sum_{z}p_{0}(z)^{2} \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t} \displaystyle=\sum_{z}p_{0}(z)\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{0,\beta t} \displaystyle=\sum_{z}p_{0}(z)k_{\beta,t}(z) \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t} \displaystyle=\sum_{z}\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z)\delta p_{\alpha^{\prime},t^{\prime}}(z) \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t,\beta t^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\sum_{z}\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z)k_{\beta^{\prime},t^{\prime}}(z) \displaystyle(V^{T}V)_{\beta t,\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\sum_{z}k_{\beta,t}(z)k_{\beta^{\prime},t^{\prime}}(z). $$

Our goal will be to calculate the expected value of each of these entries over random unitary circuits.

Diagonal Entries — To proceed, we carry out the calculation assuming signals which are sufficiently in the bulk of the RUC, such that that we can replace the brickwork circuits before and after the location of the signal with global Haar random unitaries. More specifically, for calculating the diagonal entries of $V^{T}V$ , we approximate

$$ \displaystyle p_{0}(z) \displaystyle=|\braket{z|R_{2}R_{1}|0}|^{2} \displaystyle\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle=-i\braket{z|R_{2}P_{\alpha}R_{1}|0}\braket{0|R^{\dagger}_{1}R_{2}|z}+h.c. \displaystyle k_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle=|\braket{z|R_{2}P_{\alpha}R_{1}|0}|^{2} $$

where $R_{1},R_{2}\sim\text{Haar}(2^{N})$ and average over $R_{1}$ , $R_{2}$ . We can compute this average by using tensor network diagrams, shown for the expressions above in Fig. S5, as well as Weingarten calculus [22, 23], explained graphically in Fig. S6. Letting $d=2^{N}$ , this yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{0,0} \displaystyle=\frac{2}{d}+O(\frac{1}{d^{2}}) \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{\alpha t,\alpha t} \displaystyle=\frac{2}{d}+O(\frac{1}{d^{2}}), \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{\beta t,\beta t} \displaystyle=\frac{2}{d}+O(\frac{1}{d^{2}}), $$

where we have expanded the results in $\frac{1}{d}$ . Fluctuations about these means can be shown to be suppressed by a factor of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}$ though a similar calculation, and are thus exponentially smaller. Thus, even when not averaging over random circuits, we expect these expectations to hold for individual circuit instances.

Off-diagonal Entries — Results for each of these entries are given in Eqs. (II.125), (II.126), (II.141), (II.144), and (II.146). For off-diagonal terms $(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t}$ and $(V^{T}V)_{0,\beta t}$ , we continue to use the diagrams in Fig. S5. This yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{0,\beta t} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}+O(\frac{1}{d^{3}}) $$

Fluctuations about these means are suppressed by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}$ . As $\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t}=0$ , we further compute the variance exactly to quantify the magnitude of these entries,

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Var}\bigg((V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t}\bigg)=\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}\bigg((V^{T}V)^{2}_{0,\alpha t}\bigg)=\frac{4}{d^{3}}+O(\frac{1}{d^{4}}). $$

So, the magnitude of $(V^{T}V)_{0,\alpha t}$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{2}{d}$ , or smaller by a factor of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}$ with respect to entries on the diagonal.

We now calculate the expected value of $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}$ . Here, to account for the fact that the circuit separating signals $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ , $\theta_{\alpha}^{\prime}(t^{\prime})$ may not be deep enough to be considered a Haar random unitary, we consider the modified expressions

$$ \displaystyle\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle=-i\braket{z|R_{2}(RUC)P_{\alpha}R_{1}|0}\braket{0|R^{\dagger}_{1}(RUC)^{\dagger}R^{\dagger}_{2}|z}+h.c., \displaystyle\delta p_{\alpha^{\prime},t^{\prime}}(z) \displaystyle=-i\braket{z|R_{2}P_{\alpha^{\prime}}(RUC)R_{1}|0}\braket{0|R^{\dagger}_{1}(RUC)^{\dagger}R^{\dagger}_{2}|z}+h.c., $$

where $RUC$ is the brickwork random local unitary circuit separating $P_{\alpha}$ and $P_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ . For simplicity of analysis, we assume $P_{\alpha}$ and $P_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ to be single-qubit operators. This is illustrated in Fig. S7(a). Specifically, if signals $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ , $\theta_{\alpha}^{\prime}(t^{\prime})$ are $\tau$ layers apart in the circuit (i.e. $t^{\prime}=t+\tau$ ), then RUC is a brickwork circuit of depth $\tau$ . We aim to average $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}$ over both $R_{1},R_{2}$ and the gates of $RUC$ . From a similar calculation as before,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\bigg(\textrm{Tr}(RUC^{\dagger}P_{\alpha}RUCP_{\alpha^{\prime}})+c.c.\bigg) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\bigg(\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})+\textrm{Tr}(P^{*}_{\alpha}(\tau)P^{*}_{\alpha^{\prime}})\bigg) $$

where in the second line, we have defined

$$ \displaystyle RUC^{\dagger}P_{\alpha}RUC\equiv P_{\alpha}(\tau). $$

Moreover, we have used that for Pauli operators, $P=P^{\dagger}$ . Now,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{RUC}\frac{1}{d^{2}}\bigg(\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})+\textrm{Tr}(P^{*}_{\alpha}(\tau)P^{*}_{\alpha^{\prime}})\bigg)\sim\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha})\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha^{\prime}})=0, $$

where the average over the local gates of the RUC can be performed using a tensor network diagram and the rules of Fig. S6. Thus, we have

$$ \displaystyle E_{R_{1},R_{2},RUC}(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}=0. $$

We now explicitly compute the variance of this entry to quantify its magnitude.

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}((V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t})^{2}=\frac{d^{-2}}{d^{2}}\bigg(\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})+\textrm{Tr}(P^{*}_{\alpha}(\tau)P^{*}_{\alpha^{\prime}})\bigg)^{2}+O(\frac{1}{d^{3}}), $$

where we have explicitly included $d^{-2}$ to normalize the trace, which we expect to be $O(d^{2})$ . Importantly, if we were to assume a Haar random unitary between $P_{\alpha}$ and $P_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ , or $P_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ not within the lightcone of $P_{\alpha}$ , then the variance would be $O(\frac{1}{d^{3}})$ . Thus, the $O(\frac{1}{d^{2}})$ component quantifies how a local brickwork RUC affects correlation between two different signals which are causally related.

We can expand $\bigg(\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})+\textrm{Tr}(P^{*}_{\alpha}(\tau)P^{*}_{\alpha^{\prime}})\bigg)^{2}$ = $\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})^{2}+2\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})\textrm{Tr}(P^{*}_{\alpha}(\tau)P^{*}_{\alpha^{\prime}})+\textrm{Tr}(P^{*}_{\alpha}(\tau)P^{*}_{\alpha^{\prime}})^{2}$ . We can simplify this expansion by noting that

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{Tr}(P^{*}_{\alpha}(\tau)P^{*}_{\alpha^{\prime}}) \displaystyle=\textrm{Tr}(P^{\dagger}_{\alpha^{\prime}}P^{\dagger}_{\alpha}(\tau)) \displaystyle=\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}}), $$

where we have used the cyclic property of the trace, as as well the hermiticity of Pauli operators.

So, we have the leading order term

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2},RUC}((V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t})^{2}=4\mathbb{E}_{RUC}\frac{d^{-2}\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})^{2}}{d^{2}}. $$

A tensor network diagram for this term is depicted in Fig. S7.
