Using techniques pioneered in Refs. [24] and [25], we can evaluate the average of this quantity over local gates in the brickwork RUC by mapping to a spin model. We find it convenient to state the final answer in terms of lightcone coordinates,

$$ \displaystyle u\coloneqq\frac{(t+x+1)}{2},\,\,v\coloneqq\frac{(t-x+1)}{2},\,\,t=u+v-1,\,\,x=u-v, $$

as shown in Fig. S7(c), as well as for arbitary local dimension $q$ . Here, $x$ is the space coordinate, while $t$ is the vertical, or time coordinate. We assume $t=1$ at the start of the circuit and $t=\tau$ at the end.

Then, similar to the result in Ref. [24],

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{RUC}\bigg(d^{-2}\textrm{Tr}(P_{\alpha}(\tau)P_{\alpha^{\prime}})\bigg) \displaystyle=\frac{q^{2}}{q^{4}-1}\bigg(\frac{q}{q^{2}+1}\bigg)^{2\tau-2}\sum_{u=0}^{l_{u}-1}\sum_{v=0}^{l_{v}-1}\bigg(\frac{1}{q}\bigg)^{2\tau-2u-2v}\bigg[\begin{pmatrix}\tau-1\\
v\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\tau-1\\
u\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}\tau-1\\
v-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\tau-1\\
u-1\end{pmatrix}\bigg], \displaystyle\equiv D(l_{u},l_{v}), $$

where $(l_{u},l_{v})$ is the separation between $P_{\alpha}$ and $P_{\alpha}^{\prime}$ in spacetime coordinates. The second term in brackets vanishes when $u-1$ or $v-1$ is less than $0$ . $D(l_{u},l_{v})$ thus quantifies the leading-order variance of the correlation between two spacetime-separated operators in a local brickwork RUC. As we work with qubits, $q=2$ . So, we finally have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2},RUC}((V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t})^{2}=\frac{4D(l_{u},l_{v})}{d^{2}}+O(\frac{1}{d^{3}}), $$

and $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}$ has fluctuations with magnitude $\frac{2\sqrt{D(l_{u},l_{v})}}{d}$ . Upon first glance, this is the same order in $\frac{1}{d}$ as the diagonal terms Eq. (II.123). However, examining Eq. (II.140), we can see that it is only nonzero within the lightcone of $P_{\alpha}$ , and it is furthermore exponentially suppressed when moving further away from $P_{\alpha}$ in time and space. In practice, as our signals are separated by at least two brickwork layers, we find that off-diagonal terms are small compared to the diagonal.

We follow a similar procedure for $(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}$ , using

$$ \displaystyle\delta p_{\alpha,t}(z) \displaystyle=-i\braket{z|R_{2}(RUC)P_{\alpha}R_{1}|0}\braket{0|R^{\dagger}_{1}(RUC)^{\dagger}R^{\dagger}_{2}|z}+h.c., \displaystyle k_{\beta^{\prime},t^{\prime}}(z) \displaystyle=|\braket{z|R_{2}P_{\beta^{\prime}}(RUC)R_{1}|0}|^{2}. $$

This yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2},RUC}(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}=0. $$

Furthermore, the magnitude of fluctuations of $(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}$ is suppressed by a factor of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}$ with respect to diagonal entries of $(V^{T}V)$ .

We finally compute $(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\beta t}$ , using the same ideas as before. We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\beta t}=\frac{1+d^{-2}|\textrm{Tr}(P_{\beta}(t)P_{\beta^{\prime}})|^{2}}{d}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{d^{2}}\bigg). $$

Now, if $RUC$ were global Haar-random, or if $P_{\beta}$ and $P_{\beta^{\prime}}$ are not within each others’ light cones, then we would have $\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2}}(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\beta t}=\frac{1}{d}+O(\frac{1}{d^{3}})$ . Thus, the difference that the local RUC imparts lies in the $|\textrm{Tr}(P_{\beta}(t)P_{\beta^{\prime}})|^{2}$ term. From our previous calculations, we can write

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{R_{1},R_{2},RUC}(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\beta t}=\frac{1+D(l_{u},l_{v})}{d}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{d^{2}}\bigg), $$

where $(l_{u},l_{v})$ is the separation between $P_{\beta}$ and $P_{\beta}^{\prime}$ in lightcone coordinates (see Fig. S7). $D(l_{u},l_{v})$ is defined in Eq. (II.140). $D(l_{u},l_{v})$ is exponentially suppressed the further $P_{\beta^{\prime}}$ and $P_{\beta}$ are from each other. So, in practice, with two local brickwork layers between signals, this correction is quite small and $(V^{T}V)_{\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime},\beta t}\approx\frac{1}{d}$ . Moreover, fluctuations about this mean are suppressed by a factor of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}$ .

Invertibility analysis— Gathering our results from above, for enough layers between signal operators, we expect $V^{T}V$ to have the following entries

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}(V^{T}V)\approx\bordermatrix{&0&\beta t_{1}&\beta t_{2}&\beta t_{3}&\cdots&\alpha t_{1}&\alpha t_{2}&\alpha t_{3}&\cdots\cr 0&\tfrac{2}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\cdots&0&0&0&\cdots\cr\beta t_{1}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{2}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\cdots&0&0&0&\cdots\cr\beta t_{2}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{2}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\cdots&0&0&0&\cdots\cr\beta t_{3}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{1}{d}&\tfrac{2}{d}&\cdots&0&0&0&\cdots\cr\vdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\ddots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\ddots\cr\alpha t_{1}&0&0&0&0&\cdots&\tfrac{2}{d}&0&0&\cdots\cr\alpha t_{2}&0&0&0&0&\cdots&0&\tfrac{2}{d}&0&\cdots\cr\alpha t_{3}&0&0&0&0&\cdots&0&0&\tfrac{2}{d}&\cdots\cr\vdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\ddots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\ddots\cr} $$

Matrix elements between $\beta^{\prime}t^{\prime}$ and $\beta t$ and have corrections that are exponentially small in the spacetime distance of $\gamma_{\beta^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})$ , $\gamma_{\beta}(t)$ . Moreover, fluctuations about these means are generally of order $\frac{1}{d^{3/2}}$ , with the exception of $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}$ — in this case, $(V^{T}V)_{\alpha^{\prime}t^{\prime},\alpha t}$ has fluctuations of magnitude $O(\frac{1}{d})$ that also decrease exponentially with the spacetime distance of the signals $\theta_{\alpha^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})$ , $\theta_{\alpha}(t)$ . We omit these exponentially small corrections in Eq. (II.147). Exponentially small fluctuations indicate that even when using a single random unitary circuit instance, $V^{T}V$ should behave like its mean.

Now, Eq. (II.147) is invertible: its upper left block is a rank-one update of the identity, while its lower right block is diagonal. For a single circuit instance, the realized $V^{T}V$ will only have small— in general, exponentially small– perturbations to Eq. (II.147). This, we expect it to be invertible [8].

### II.5 Ergodic Hamiltonian evolution

Rather than using local RUC layers, our sensing protocol can also use layers of ergodic Hamiltonian evolution [26], as illustrated in Fig. S3. We can still run the same estimation procedure for coherent and incoherent signals described in Section II.4. Intuitively, this is because we expect local Hamiltonian dynamics to be roughly equivalent to shallow layers of a nearest neighbor brickwork RUC.

To be specific, a Hamiltonian $H$ is chosen for the entire protocol and “turned on” in between signal accumulation layers. We choose a reasonable evolution time $\tau$ , and the unitary $e^{-iH\tau}$ is implemented between signals. This can be achieved, for example, by selectively echoing out the Hamiltonian while probing desired signals [27, 28].

At the end of the procedure, we perform measurements in the computational basis as usual. Our output probability distribution is still defined by Eq. (II.108), with definitions in Eqs. (II.105), (II.106), and (II.107). In this case, we just replace unitary layers by evolution under a single Hamiltonian $H$

$$ \displaystyle U_{i}\rightarrow\exp(-iH\tau), $$

where $\tau$ is a chosen period of evolution to ensure sufficient scrambling. The data analysis protocol is identical to Section II.4: we compute Eqs. (II.105), (II.106), and (II.107) using classical simulation of the Hamiltonian dynamics, and construct the estimator Eq. (II.111) for coherent and incoherent signals.

To test this protocol, we choose to evolve under the mixed-field Ising model with Kim-Huse parameters [29] and periodic boundary conditions,

$$ \displaystyle H=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}Z_{i+1}-h_{x}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}-h_{z}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i},\;\;(h_{x},h_{z})=\bigg(\frac{\sqrt{5}+5}{8},\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{4}\bigg). $$

We begin with an initial product state of $\ket{+}_{y}^{\otimes N}$ , where $\ket{+}_{y}$ is the $+1$ eigenstate of Pauli $Y$ . This ensures that the initial state is at infinite temperature, and hence the dynamics explores a large effective Hilbert space. The results are shown in Fig. S4(e,f), for an evolution time $\tau=5$ . The performance is comparable to the local RUC protocol, with estimators faithfully reconstructing sparse signals and maintaining SQL scaling in the presence of nonzero readout error. We leave a more extensive optimization of these estimators in the case of Hamiltonian evolution to future work.
